messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Public Defender
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 70

He is a 68-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life as a public defender, a job that taught him how to sit across from frightened people, listen carefully, and keep his own feelings contained long enough to be useful. For years, that discipline has served him well. He is known as calm, meticulous, and difficult to rattle. At home, he was different in the best possible way: softer, more playful, deeply attached to his wife, the person who made his long hours and heavy caseload feel bearable.

The trauma begins not with a single dramatic moment but with the gradual loss of the life he had assumed would continue. His wife becomes ill unexpectedly, and at first he responds the way he has always responded to problems: by researching, organizing appointments, asking precise questions, and trying to stay ahead of what is coming. He remembers the first time the doctor used language that made his stomach tighten. He does not recall crying then. He recalls writing everything down, insisting on being practical, and driving home in silence while his wife slept in the passenger seat, small and tired beside him.

As her condition worsens, he becomes her advocate in a way that feels painfully familiar and entirely new. He knows how to challenge authority, how to ask for clarification, how to push when an answer is evasive. Yet none of that prepares him for the helplessness of watching the person he loves fade in front of him. He begins spending more time at hospitals than at his office, carrying files with one hand and his worry with the other. His colleagues notice that he is still functioning, still appearing in court, but he is sharper in a brittle way and more forgetful than he used to be. He rereads the same documents, loses track of conversations, and finds himself staring at ordinary things without absorbing them.

When she dies, he is not sure what to do with the silence that follows. He describes the house afterward as “too organized,” because everything remains where she left it, including the sweater draped over the chair and the tea mug on the counter. In the first weeks, he keeps expecting to hear her footsteps or the sound of her voice calling from another room. He still turns his head when he enters the house, as if she might be there. Instead, he is met with absence so complete that it feels physical.

Since her death, he lives as though part of him has been left behind in the hospital room and never returned. He continues to work, but his concentration is unreliable. In court, he sometimes notices his mind slipping away from the case and back to the last days of her illness, back to the monitor alarms, the smell of antiseptic, the look on her face when she tried to reassure him. He avoids certain hallways in the hospital and will not drive past the building unless necessary. At night, he sleeps lightly and wakes often, sometimes with the sense that something terrible has just happened, and for a moment he does not know whether he is in the present or in the months before her death.

He carries a private anger that he rarely speaks aloud. He is angry at the disease, at the doctors who could not save her, at himself for not noticing sooner or doing enough, even though he can name the irrationality of these thoughts as easily as he can name legal standards in a courtroom. His grief turns on him in unexpected ways: he snaps at minor inconveniences, then feels ashamed. He declines invitations from friends and family because he does not want to answer the question “How are you?” with the truth. On the rare evenings when he sits alone, he watches the same photographs over and over, touching her face in the images as if contact might preserve what memory cannot.

He remains proud of his work, but even that identity feels altered. As a public defender, he still shows up for the vulnerable and accused, yet he notices that his empathy has become more painful than before. Cases involving family separation, illness, or sudden death leave him unsettled in a way they never used to. He can still speak with authority, still organize an argument, but afterward he returns to an empty home and feels the weight of being the one who remains. He lives with a steady sense that his world changed in one irreversible season and never fully recovered its shape.
